title: AC Power
description: Average, reactive and apparent power of every element, power factor and power-factor correction in randomized circuits.

study.title: Complex power
study.body: For an element with peak phasors $\mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{I}$ (passive reference: current into the + terminal) the complex power is $\mathbf{S} = \tfrac12\mathbf{V}\mathbf{I}^*$. Its real part is the average power $P$ (W), its imaginary part the reactive power $Q$ (var) and its magnitude the apparent power $|\mathbf{S}|$ (VA). With rms phasors drop the ½.

study.title: R, L and C
study.body: Only resistors absorb average power: $P_R = \tfrac12 I_m^2R$. Inductors absorb reactive power ($Q_L = \tfrac12 I_m^2\omega L > 0$), capacitors deliver it ($Q_C = -\tfrac12 I_m^2/(\omega C) < 0$). Complex power is conserved: the sources deliver exactly the sum of what the elements absorb, separately for $P$ and for $Q$.

study.title: Power factor
study.body: $\text{pf} = \cos\theta = P/|\mathbf{S}|$ with $\theta = \theta_v - \theta_i$ the angle of the load impedance. An inductive load ($Q > 0$, current lags the voltage) has a **lagging** power factor; a capacitive load ($Q < 0$, current leads) a **leading** one. The power triangle links them: $Q = P\tan\theta$.

study.title: Power-factor correction
study.body: A capacitor in parallel with an inductive load leaves $P$ unchanged and supplies reactive power, so the source current drops. To go from $\theta_{old}$ to $\theta_{new}$ the capacitor must supply $\Delta Q = P(\tan\theta_{old} - \tan\theta_{new})$; with peak voltage $V_m$ across it, $|Q_C| = \tfrac12\omega CV_m^2 = \omega CV_{rms}^2$.

study.title: Pitfalls
study.body:
- With peak phasors every power has a factor ½; with rms phasors it does not.
- $Q$ is signed: a capacitor absorbs negative reactive power, and a source feeding a capacitive load *delivers* negative $Q$.
- The power factor alone does not tell leading from lagging: always state which.
- $P \ne \tfrac12 V_mI_m$ unless the load is purely resistive.

steps.title: Complex power in one line
steps.body: Solve the circuit with phasors, then for every element compute $\mathbf{S} = \tfrac12\mathbf{V}\mathbf{I}^*$ (peak phasors, passive reference). $P = \text{Re}\,\mathbf{S}$ is what heats resistors; $Q = \text{Im}\,\mathbf{S}$ sloshes back and forth between the source and the L's and C's.
steps.formula: P_R = \tfrac12 I_m^2R,\qquad Q_L = \tfrac12 I_m^2X_L,\qquad Q_C = -\tfrac12 I_m^2X_C

steps.prompt: The source is $v_s(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(2\pi\cdot {{f}}\,t)$ V (peak value).

ask.prompt: Find the average power absorbed by $R$.
Find the reactive power absorbed by $L$.
ask.explanation: $X_L = \omega L$ = {{XL|Ω}}, $|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$ = {{Zm|Ω}}, $I_m = V_m/|Z|$ = {{I_L1|A}}. $Q_L = \tfrac12 I_m^2X_L$ = **{{Q_L1|var}}** (positive: an inductor absorbs reactive power).

ask.prompt: Find the apparent power $|\mathbf{S}|$ delivered by the source.
ask.explanation: $I_m = V_m/|Z|$ = {{Vm|V}} / {{Zm|Ω}} = {{I_Vs|A}}, so $|\mathbf{S}| = \tfrac12V_mI_m$ = **{{S_Vs|VA}}**. Check: $\sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}$ with $P$ = {{P_R1|W}} and $Q$ = {{Q_L1|var}}.

ask.prompt: Find the average power delivered by the source.
ask.explanation: The inductor absorbs no average power, so the source delivers what $R$ absorbs: $I_m = V_m/|Z|$ = {{I_Vs|A}}, $P = \tfrac12I_m^2R$ = **{{P_Vs|W}}**. (Not $\tfrac12V_mI_m$ = {{S_Vs|VA}}: that is the apparent power.)

steps.prompt: The circuit is in sinusoidal steady state. Tap every element that absorbs **zero average power**.
steps.explanation: For an ideal inductor or capacitor the current is 90° out of phase with the voltage, so $P = \tfrac12V_mI_m\cos(\pm 90°) = 0$. They only exchange reactive power. Both resistors carry current, so both absorb $P = \tfrac12I_m^2R > 0$.

steps.prompt: A capacitor carries a sinusoidal current of amplitude $I_m$. Which statement about its power is correct?
steps.explanation: With $\mathbf{V} = Z_C\mathbf{I} = -jX_C\mathbf{I}$: $\mathbf{S} = \tfrac12\mathbf{V}\mathbf{I}^* = -j\tfrac12X_C I_m^2$. The real part (average power) is 0 and the reactive power is negative: a capacitor *supplies* reactive power.

steps.title: Leading or lagging?
steps.body: The power factor is $\cos\theta$ with $\theta = \theta_v - \theta_i$, the angle of the load impedance. Inductive load: current lags, $Q > 0$, **lagging** pf. Capacitive load: current leads, $Q < 0$, **leading** pf. A pf of 1 means a purely resistive load.

steps.prompt: The source is $v_s(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(2\pi\cdot {{f}}\,t)$ V (peak value).

ask.prompt: Find the power factor seen by the source.
ask.explanation: $Z = R - jX_C$ with $X_C = 1/(\omega C)$ = {{XC|Ω}}, so $|Z|$ = {{Zm|Ω}} and pf $= R/|Z|$ = {{R||3}}/{{Zm||3}} = **{{pf_Vs||3}}** (leading: the load is capacitive).

ask.prompt: Find the reactive power absorbed by the capacitor (signed, in var).
Find the reactive power **delivered** by the source (signed, in var).
ask.explanation: Reactive power is conserved: the source delivers what the elements absorb, $Q_s = Q_R + Q_C$ = 0 + ({{Q_C1|var}}) = **{{Q_Vs|var}}**. It is negative: the capacitor actually pushes reactive power back into the source.

steps.prompt: The source is $v_s(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(2\pi\cdot {{f}}\,t)$ V (peak value). Is the power factor seen by the source leading or lagging?
steps.explanation: $X = \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}$ = {{XL||3}} − {{XC||3}} = {{XL-XC||3}} Ω. $X > 0$ means an inductive load (lagging pf, $Q > 0$); $X < 0$ a capacitive load (leading pf, $Q < 0$). Here $Q$ = {{Q_Vs|var}} and pf = {{pf_Vs||3}}.

steps.prompt: In any circuit, the reactive power delivered by the sources equals the sum of the reactive powers absorbed by the inductors and capacitors (counting the capacitors’ negative values).
steps.explanation: Complex power is conserved ($\sum\mathbf{S}_{delivered} = \sum\mathbf{S}_{absorbed}$), so both its real part (average power: resistors) and its imaginary part (reactive power: $Q_L > 0$, $Q_C < 0$) balance separately.

steps.prompt: The source is $v_s(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(2\pi\cdot {{f}}\,t)$ V (peak value).

ask.prompt: Find the average power absorbed by $R_1$.
ask.explanation: Load seen by the source: $R_1 + Z_C\parallel(R_2 + j\omega L)$ with $Z_C = -j${{XC||3}} Ω and $j\omega L = j${{XL||3}} Ω. The source current amplitude is {{I_R1|A}}, so $P_{R_1} = \tfrac12I_m^2R_1$ = **{{P_R1|W}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the average power absorbed by $R_2$.
ask.explanation: The voltage across $C$ has amplitude {{V_C1|V}}; it drives $R_2 + j\omega L$, $|Z_2|$ = {{sqrt(R2^2+XL^2)|Ω}}, so $I_{m2}$ = {{I_R2|A}} and $P_{R_2} = \tfrac12I_{m2}^2R_2$ = **{{P_R2|W}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the reactive power absorbed by $C$ (signed).
Find the reactive power delivered by the source (signed).
ask.explanation: Conservation of complex power: $Q_s = Q_L + Q_C$ = {{Q_L1|var}} + ({{Q_C1|var}}) = **{{Q_Vs|var}}** ($Q_L = \tfrac12I_{m2}^2\omega L$ with $I_{m2}$ = {{I_L1|A}}).

ask.prompt: Find the power factor seen by the source.
ask.explanation: $P = P_{R_1} + P_{R_2}$ = {{P_Vs|W}}, $Q = Q_L + Q_C$ = {{Q_Vs|var}}, $|\mathbf{S}| = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}$ = {{S_Vs|VA}}. pf $= P/|\mathbf{S}|$ = **{{pf_Vs||3}}** (lagging if $Q > 0$, leading if $Q < 0$).

steps.prompt: Here the source phasor is an **rms** value: $\mathbf{V}_s$ = {{Vr}}∠0° V rms at $f$ = {{f|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Find the rms current.
Find the average power absorbed by the load.
ask.explanation: With rms phasors there is no ½: $I_{rms}$ = {{I_Vs|A}}, $P = I_{rms}^2R$ = **{{P_Vs|W}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the reactive power absorbed by the load.
ask.explanation: $Q = I_{rms}^2X_L$ = ({{I_Vs|A}})² · {{XL|Ω}} = **{{Q_Vs|var}}** (rms phasors: no ½).

ask.prompt: Find the apparent power.
ask.explanation: $|\mathbf{S}| = V_{rms}I_{rms}$ = {{Vr|V}} · {{I_Vs|A}} = **{{S_Vs|VA}}**.

steps.prompt: A load absorbs $P$ = {{P|W}} at a power factor of {{pf}} **lagging**.

ask.prompt: Find its reactive power $Q$ (signed).
ask.explanation: $\theta = \arccos({{pf}})$ = {{deg(th)|°}}, positive because the pf is lagging (inductive). $Q = P\tan\theta$ = {{P|W}} · {{tan(th)||3}} = **{{Q|var}}**.

ask.prompt: Find its apparent power $|\mathbf{S}|$.
ask.explanation: $|\mathbf{S}| = P/\text{pf}$ = {{P|W}}/{{pf}} = **{{S|VA}}** (the hypotenuse of the power triangle).

ask.prompt: The load voltage is 230 V rms. Find the rms load current.
ask.explanation: $|\mathbf{S}| = P/\text{pf}$ = {{S|VA}} and $|\mathbf{S}| = V_{rms}I_{rms}$, so $I_{rms}$ = {{S|VA}}/230 V = **{{S/230|A}}**.

steps.prompt: A load has apparent power $|\mathbf{S}|$ = {{S|VA}} at a power factor of {{pf}} **leading**. What is its reactive power $Q$?
steps.explanation: $|Q| = |\mathbf{S}|\sin\theta = |\mathbf{S}|\sqrt{1 - \text{pf}^2}$ = {{S*sqrt(1-pf^2)|var}}. Leading means capacitive, so $Q$ is negative: **{{-S*sqrt(1-pf^2)|var}}**. ($|\mathbf{S}|\cdot\text{pf}$ = {{S*pf|W}} is $P$, not $Q$.)

steps.prompt: The source is $v_s(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(2\pi\cdot {{f}}\,t)$ V (peak value). Load 1 is $R_1$ in series with $L$; load 2 is $R_2$ in series with $C$.

ask.prompt: Find the total average power delivered by the source.
ask.explanation: Each load sees the full source voltage. Load 1: $I_1 = V_m/|R_1 + j\omega L|$ = {{I_R1|A}}, $P_1 = \tfrac12I_1^2R_1$ = {{P_R1|W}}. Load 2: $I_2 = V_m/|R_2 - jX_C|$ = {{I_R2|A}}, $P_2$ = {{P_R2|W}}. $P = P_1 + P_2$ = **{{P_Vs|W}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the total reactive power delivered by the source (signed).
ask.explanation: $Q_1 = \tfrac12I_1^2X_L$ = {{Q_L1|var}} ($X_L$ = {{XL|Ω}}), $Q_2 = -\tfrac12I_2^2X_C$ = {{Q_C1|var}} ($X_C$ = {{XC|Ω}}). Complex powers add: $Q$ = **{{Q_Vs|var}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the power factor seen by the source.
ask.explanation: $P$ = {{P_R1|W}} + {{P_R2|W}} = {{P_Vs|W}}, $Q$ = {{Q_L1|var}} + ({{Q_C1|var}}) = {{Q_Vs|var}}. $|\mathbf{S}|$ = {{S_Vs|VA}}, pf $= P/|\mathbf{S}|$ = **{{pf_Vs||3}}** (lagging if $Q > 0$, leading if $Q < 0$).

ask.prompt: Find the amplitude of the source current.
ask.explanation: Add the complex powers: $|\mathbf{S}| = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}$ = {{S_Vs|VA}} with $P$ = {{P_Vs|W}}, $Q$ = {{Q_Vs|var}}. Then $|\mathbf{S}| = \tfrac12V_mI_m$ gives $I_m = 2|\mathbf{S}|/V_m$ = **{{I_Vs|A}}** — less than {{I_R1|A}} + {{I_R2|A}}, because the two load currents are not in phase.

steps.prompt: Match each element or load with the signs of the power it absorbs.
steps.explanation: $\mathbf{S} = \tfrac12|\mathbf{I}|^2Z = \tfrac12I_m^2(R + jX)$: $P$ comes from $R$ and the sign of $Q$ is the sign of $X$ ($X_L = \omega L > 0$, $X_C = -1/(\omega C) < 0$).

steps.prompt: The source is $i_s(t) = {{Im}}\cos(2\pi\cdot {{f}}\,t)$ A (peak value).

ask.prompt: Find the amplitude of the voltage across the source.
ask.explanation: $Z = R\parallel Z_C$ with $X_C$ = {{XC|Ω}}: $|Z| = \frac{RX_C}{\sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2}}$ = {{Zp|Ω}}. $V_m = I_m|Z|$ = **{{V_R1|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the average power delivered by the source.
ask.explanation: Only $R$ absorbs average power, and it has the full voltage $V_m = I_m|Z|$ = {{V_R1|V}} across it: $P = \frac{V_m^2}{2R}$ = **{{P_Is|W}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the reactive power absorbed by $C$ (signed).
Find the power factor seen by the source.
ask.explanation: $P$ = {{P_Is|W}}, $Q$ = {{Q_C1|var}}, $|\mathbf{S}| = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$ = {{S_Is|VA}}: pf = **{{pf_Is||3}}** leading. For a parallel RC: pf $= X_C/\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}$.

steps.prompt: The source is $v_s(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(2\pi\cdot {{f}}\,t)$ V (peak value). True or false: the source delivers more reactive power (in var) than average power (in W).
steps.explanation: Both powers come from the same current: $Q/P = \frac{\frac12I_m^2X_L}{\frac12I_m^2R} = X_L/R$ = {{XL||3}}/{{R||3}} = {{XL/R||3}}. Here $P$ = {{P_Vs|W}} and $Q$ = {{Q_Vs|var}}.

steps.title: Correcting the power factor
steps.body: Put a capacitor **in parallel** with the load. The load voltage, and so the load's $P$ and $Q_{load}$, do not change; the capacitor adds $Q_C = -\tfrac12\omega CV_m^2$. Choose $C$ so that $Q_{load} + Q_C = P\tan\theta_{new}$.

steps.prompt: The source $v_s(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(2\pi\cdot {{f}}\,t)$ V (peak) feeds an inductive load.

ask.prompt: Find the power factor of the load.
Find the capacitance that, connected in parallel with the load, raises the power factor to {{pft}} lagging.
ask.explanation: Load: $I_m$ = {{I_Vs|A}}, $P = \tfrac12I_m^2R$ = {{P_Vs|W}}, $Q = \tfrac12I_m^2X_L$ = {{Q_Vs|var}}. Target: $Q_{new} = P\tan(\arccos {{pft}})$ = {{Qn|var}}. The capacitor supplies $\Delta Q$ = {{Q_Vs-Qn|var}} $= \tfrac12\omega CV_m^2$, so $C = \frac{2\Delta Q}{\omega V_m^2}$ = **{{Cpf|F}}**.

steps.prompt: The source $v_s(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(2\pi\cdot {{f}}\,t)$ V (peak) feeds an R–L load with a correction capacitor $C$ in parallel.

ask.prompt: Find the power factor seen by the source.
ask.explanation: Load alone: $P$ = {{P_R1|W}}, $Q_L$ = {{Q_L1|var}} (pf {{P_R1/sqrt(P_R1^2+Q_L1^2)||3}}). Capacitor: $Q_C = -\tfrac12\omega CV_m^2$ = {{Q_C1|var}}. Total $Q$ = {{Q_Vs|var}}, so pf $= P/\sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$ = **{{pf_Vs||3}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the amplitude of the source current.
ask.explanation: $P$ = {{P_Vs|W}} (unchanged), $Q = Q_L + Q_C$ = {{Q_L1|var}} + ({{Q_C1|var}}) = {{Q_Vs|var}}, $|\mathbf{S}|$ = {{S_Vs|VA}}. $I_m = 2|\mathbf{S}|/V_m$ = **{{I_Vs|A}}**, down from {{I_R1|A}} without the capacitor.

ask.prompt: Find the average power delivered by the source.
ask.explanation: The capacitor absorbs no average power and does not change the load voltage, so $P$ is still the resistor's: $I_{load} = V_m/|R + j\omega L|$ = {{I_R1|A}}, $P = \tfrac12I_{load}^2R$ = **{{P_Vs|W}}**.

steps.prompt: $v_s(t) = {{Vm}}\cos(2\pi\cdot {{f}}\,t)$ V (peak). With the capacitor connected, is the power factor seen by the source leading or lagging?
steps.explanation: The load absorbs $Q_L$ = {{Q_L1|var}}; the capacitor supplies $|Q_C| = \tfrac12\omega CV_m^2$ = {{-Q_C1|var}}. The net $Q$ = {{Q_Vs|var}}: positive means lagging, negative means the capacitor is too large and the pf is leading (pf = {{pf_Vs||3}}).

steps.prompt: An industrial load absorbs {{P|W}} at pf {{pf1}} lagging from a {{Vr}} V rms, {{f}} Hz supply. The pf must be raised to {{pf2}} lagging with a parallel capacitor.

ask.prompt: Find the reactive power the capacitor must supply (magnitude).
ask.explanation: $Q_{old} = P\tan\theta_{old}$ = {{P|W}} · {{t1||3}} = {{P*t1|var}}, $Q_{new} = P\tan\theta_{new}$ = {{P*t2|var}}. The capacitor supplies the difference: **{{dQ|var}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the capacitance.
ask.explanation: $\Delta Q = P(\tan\theta_{old} - \tan\theta_{new})$ = {{dQ|var}}. With rms voltage $|Q_C| = \omega CV_{rms}^2$, so $C = \frac{\Delta Q}{\omega V_{rms}^2}$ = {{dQ||3}} / ({{2*pi*f||4}} · {{Vr}}²) = **{{Cc|F}}**.

steps.prompt: A load keeps the same average power and voltage while its power factor is corrected from {{pf1}} to {{pf2}}. Find the ratio $I_{new}/I_{old}$ of the line-current amplitudes.
steps.explanation: $P = \tfrac12V_mI_m\,\text{pf}$ with $P$ and $V_m$ fixed, so $I_m \propto 1/\text{pf}$: $I_{new}/I_{old} = \text{pf}_{old}/\text{pf}_{new}$ = {{pf1}}/{{pf2}} = **{{pf1/pf2||3}}**. The line losses $\propto I^2$ drop to {{100*(pf1/pf2)^2|%}}.

steps.prompt: Why do utilities want large inductive loads to correct their power factor?
options: For the same average power, a higher pf means less line current, so smaller $I^2R$ losses and smaller cables and transformers
The capacitor increases the average power the load can absorb from the same supply
The capacitor makes the load consume less energy in its own resistance
A capacitor in parallel raises the load voltage, which halves the losses
steps.explanation: The load's own $P$ (and energy use) is unchanged. What changes is the reactive power supplied through the lines: with less $Q$ the current amplitude $I_m = 2P/(V_m\,\text{pf})$ drops, so the utility's line losses and equipment ratings ($|\mathbf{S}|$ in VA) go down.

steps.prompt: Placing the correction capacitor in **series** with the load (instead of in parallel) works just as well, since it supplies the same reactive power.
steps.explanation: A series capacitor changes the current through, and the voltage across, the load, so the load no longer gets its rated voltage and its $P$ changes. A parallel capacitor sits across the same voltage and leaves the load untouched; only the line current changes.
